periods.analysis: We are opening this reporting arc in a red position: the rent-burdened household rate is 59.5%, well above the <=45% target and the >52% red threshold. Because this is the first quarter in the series, there is no quarter-over-quarter movement to report yet, so I am treating 59.5% as the baseline for Council and departmental follow-up. The pressure is concentrated in renter-heavy corridors around Airport Station, Harborview East, and the South Docks bus spine, where lease renewals are outpacing wage growth. Housing, Planning, and Finance have a credible workplan in motion, but the data quality note is that we need tighter alignment between ACS updates, utility-assistance intake, and local lease survey timing before we claim a trend.
periods.recommendations: Lock the 2024-Q3 value of 59.5% as the baseline in the Council packet and add a standing red-status watch item to the quarterly housing dashboard. Direct Housing staff to prioritize the next 90 days on rent-stabilization outreach in the Airport Station and South Docks census tracts, using the HarborHelp intake list and landlord registry contacts. Ask Planning to bring forward a permit-to-occupancy schedule for active affordable projects, including units expected from the Mariner Lofts, Bayline Commons, and Terminal Avenue sites.

periods.analysis: The measure moved from 59.5% to 60.0%, a +0.5 percentage point quarter-over-quarter increase, so the result remains red and is moving the wrong way. This is not a reporting surprise: Q4 lease escalations and winter utility costs typically show up first in Harborview East, North Pier, and the older garden-apartment stock near Route 3) The team did improve the reporting cycle by reconciling landlord-filed rent rolls with 1,842 HarborHelp applications, which gives us a cleaner explanation for Council even though the outcome is not where we need it. The concern is managed, but it is real: production is still lagging demand, and preservation deals are taking too long to close.
periods.recommendations: Move the preservation closing checklist to a biweekly cadence until the Bayview Arms and Alder Court transactions are either closed or escalated. Fund a Q1 landlord participation sprint for the HarborHelp bridge-rent program, with a clear target of enrolling 75 additional small-property owners along Routes 8, 14, and 3) Keep the red status visible in the executive scorecard, but pair it with the pipeline schedule so departments can show both urgency and forward motion.

periods.analysis: The rate increased again, from 60.0% to 60.4%, a +0.4 percentage point quarter-over-quarter movement, and remains red against the <=45% target. The smaller increase compared with Q4 is helpful but not yet evidence of relief; Q1 reflects both new-year rent resets and the lag before permitted units become occupied. Staff found that 312 households in the HarborHelp dataset were also on eviction-diversion waitlists, so the Housing and Human Services teams now have a better shared cohort to manage. For Council, the message is disciplined but candid: we are improving the operating model faster than the headline measure is improving.
periods.recommendations: Create one shared Q2 case-management list for the 312 overlapping HarborHelp and eviction-diversion households, with weekly status updates owned by Human Services. Ask Planning to flag any affordable-housing permits older than 45 days in review, starting with project files HV-24-118 Mariner Lofts and HV-24-203 Seaport Family Housing. Prepare a Council memo that separates near-term household stabilization from medium-term supply delivery so expectations are clear.

periods.analysis: The rate moved from 60.4% to 60.8%, another +0.4 percentage point increase, keeping the measure in red. The spring rental survey showed the strongest pressure in two-bedroom units near the airport employment district, where hospitality and logistics workers are competing with in-migrating professional households. On the operations side, the Housing team completed first-pass data validation two days ahead of the reporting deadline, which matters because Council is asking for sharper neighborhood-level accountability. The problem remains bigger than any one program, but the City is now tracking permits, preservation, and tenant stabilization in one operating rhythm rather than three separate conversations.
periods.recommendations: Add an airport-area employer cohort to the Attainable Housing Working Group, beginning with PortJet Services, Harborview Medical Logistics, and the Terminal B concessionaires. Use Q3 inclusionary-housing compliance reviews to confirm delivery dates, affordability levels, and bedroom mix for every project within a half-mile of Airport Station. Expand the eviction-diversion legal clinic from two evenings per month to four through the end of summer, with attendance reported in the next scorecard cycle.

periods.analysis: The rate rose from 60.8% to 61.1%, a +0.3 percentage point quarter-over-quarter increase, so we are still red but the pace of worsening has edged down. That slower movement is not a win yet, but it suggests the combined effect of bridge-rent support, legal clinic expansion, and faster permit routing may be starting to blunt the steepest increases. Staff cleared 27 delayed housing-plan reviews in August, including the Bayline Commons resubmittal and the 96-unit South Docks adaptive reuse file. I want us to be careful in how we frame this: departments deserve credit for execution, while Council should still see the measure as an affordability emergency.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the accelerated permit-review table through 2025-Q4 and publish a simple aging report for affordable and mixed-income files over 30, 45, and 60 days. Extend the legal clinic contract with Coastal Justice Center for one more quarter, tied to outcomes on eviction filings avoided and payment plans completed. Prepare a targeted acquisition list of naturally occurring affordable housing near Routes 14 and 22 before speculative sales accelerate.

periods.analysis: The rate increased from 61.1% to 61.4%, a +0.3 percentage point movement, and remains red. Q4 utility and insurance pass-throughs appear to be a meaningful driver again, especially in older multifamily buildings in North Pier and the Bluffside corridor. The operating picture is more organized than it was a year ago: Housing, Planning, Finance, and Human Services are now using the same monthly dashboard, and late data submissions dropped materially in the December reporting cycle. Still, with the measure 16.4 percentage points above the <=45% target, we should not soften the language for Council.
periods.recommendations: Launch a winter cost-burden intervention package by January 15, combining utility arrearage screening, rent-payment mediation, and property-owner outreach for buildings constructed before 2) Have Finance model a dedicated preservation set-aside using incremental lodging-tax growth, with scenarios ready for the budget workshop. Keep the red-status narrative tied to named actions and named geographies so the public can see where intervention is happening.

periods.analysis: The rate moved from 61.4% to 61.7%, a +0.3 percentage point increase, so the measure remains red and continues above the >52% threshold. The first-quarter pattern is consistent with lease resets and continued in-migration tied to the airport cargo expansion and seaport logistics hiring. The City’s managed response is stronger than the result: the Housing Pipeline Tracker now shows occupancy forecasts by quarter, and staff matched 418 high-risk renter households to prevention services before notices escalated. The watch item for Council is whether new affordable units scheduled for mid-2026 actually lease up to Harborview households most at risk of displacement.
periods.recommendations: Require monthly lease-up readiness meetings for projects expected to open in 2026, starting with Mariner Lofts, Seaport Family Housing, and the Harborview East TOD parcel. Pre-qualify income-eligible households from the prevention-services list so units can be filled quickly and locally when certificates of occupancy are issued. Ask the Port and major logistics employers to co-sponsor an employer-assisted housing pilot before the Q2 budget amendment.

periods.analysis: The rate increased from 61.7% to 61.9%, a +0.2 percentage point quarter-over-quarter movement, keeping the measure red but showing the smallest increase in this eight-quarter run. I would frame that carefully for Council: the direction is still unfavorable, but the rate of deterioration has slowed from +0.5 in 2024-Q4 to +0.2 in 2026-Q2. Early lease-up at Bayline Commons and faster HarborHelp approvals are likely helping at the margin, while broad market rents near the airport and waterfront continue to overwhelm household incomes. The City is financially healthy and operationally capable, but this result confirms that attainable housing needs sustained production, preservation, and tenant stabilization at the same time.
periods.recommendations: Do not declare progress until the measure stops rising; keep the status red and set a Q3 management goal of holding the rate at or below 61.9%. Extend the fast-track review lane for affordable projects and add a preservation acquisition reserve to capture at-risk buildings before sale. Bring Council a 12-month attainable-housing action calendar with named projects, expected units, prevention-service targets, and quarterly reporting deadlines.

periods.analysis: Rent burden rose from 52.1% to 52.3%, moving further from the lower-is-better target of 48%. Housing production alone has not yet reversed household pressure.
periods.recommendations: Track preservation and tenant-stabilization work alongside unit delivery; do not describe the rate as improving.
